body.heading: A jigsaw in slow motion
paragraphs: Earth’s hard outer shell is not one piece. It is a set of enormous plates — continents and ocean floor together — and they are all in motion, creeping along at a few centimetres a year.
The movement is driven from below, where hot rock in the mantle churns extremely slowly, like an unimaginably thick soup on a stove. The plates ride, collide, dive beneath each other and pull apart.

body.heading: The evidence is everywhere
paragraphs: Alfred Wegener noticed a century ago that South America and Africa fit together like torn paper, with matching fossils and rock layers on both sides of the Atlantic. He was ridiculed for suggesting the continents had drifted — and he was right.
Today there is no need to infer it. Satellites and GPS stations measure the drift directly, year by year, as surely as a ruler measures a table.

body.heading: When plates push and slip
paragraphs: Where plates collide, mountains rise: the Himalayas are still growing by several millimetres a year as India presses into Asia. Where they grind past each other or suddenly slip, earthquakes release the strain.
It is a strange and steadying thought. The solid ground of everyday life is a raft on a slow river of rock — and it has been travelling for billions of years.

takeaway: Continents drift a few centimetres a year — imperceptible in a day, but enough to open oceans and build mountain ranges over deep time.
